result.party_text: The RAD owes deference to the findings of the RPD and should apply the reasonableness standard as this Court does when reviewing RPD decisions not subject to appeal before the RAD.
result.why: The court clearly rejected the RAD's position that it owes deference to the RPD and should apply the reasonableness standard.

result.party_text: The principal issue is whether it was reasonable for the RAD to refuse to admit a 2002 grade 12 diploma as evidence not before the RPD, pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the Act.
result.why: The court acknowledges the principal issue is whether it was reasonable for the RAD to refuse to admit the diploma as evidence.

result.party_text: The diploma would confirm that the RPD unreasonably determined that the applicant failed to demonstrate his identity and that he was not credible.
result.why: The court recognizes the diploma would confirm the RPD unreasonably determined the applicant's identity and credibility.

result.party_text: The RAD applied the jurisprudence interpreting paragraph 113(a) of the Act mutatis mutandis to the interpretation of subsection 110(4).
result.why: The court notes the RAD applied jurisprudence interpreting paragraph 113(a) mutatis mutandis to subsection 110(4).

result.party_text: Paragraph 113(a) deals with the admissibility of fresh evidence before a PRRA officer that had not been before the RPD.
result.why: The court states paragraph 113(a) deals with admissibility of fresh evidence before a PRRA officer not before the RPD.

result.party_text: The RAD held that the RPD unreasonably determined that the applicant failed to satisfactorily demonstrate his identity for other reasons, but refused to admit the new evidence affecting credibility.
result.why: The RAD held the RPD unreasonably determined identity failure but refused to admit new evidence affecting credibility, which the applicant contests.

result.party_text: The applicant’s refugee claim hearing was rejected on May 1, 2013.
result.answer_quote: The RPD held that the applicant failed to satisfactorily establish his identity.
result.why: The court confirms the RPD rejected the refugee claim on May 1, 2013.

result.party_text: The RPD held that the applicant failed to satisfactorily establish his identity.
result.why: The court states the RPD held the applicant failed to satisfactorily establish his identity.

result.party_text: The applicant claimed to have arrived with some genuine documents, including his birth certificate, a 1998 school report card, as well as two school diplomas (a grade 10 diploma from 2000, and a grade 12 diploma from 2002).
result.why: The court acknowledges the applicant claimed to have arrived with the listed documents.

result.party_text: The RPD found it noteworthy to add that neither diploma had been examined by the Canada Border Services Agency [CBSA].
result.why: The court notes the RPD found neither diploma had been examined by CBSA.

result.party_text: However, only the grade 10 diploma was before the RPD.
result.why: The court states only the grade 10 diploma was before the RPD.

result.party_text: In addition to not confirming his identity, the fact that the 2002 diploma was missing could not corroborate that the applicant had studied with Bhupinder Singh until 2002.
result.why: The court confirms the missing 2002 diploma could not corroborate the applicant's study with Bhupinder Singh until 2002.

result.party_text: The applicant alleged that his grade 12 diploma had been taken by Citizenship and Immigration Canada [CIC] when he had been detained upon arrival, and that CIC failed to forward it to the RPD.
result.why: The court repeats the applicant's allegation about the diploma being taken by CIC and not forwarded to the RPD.

result.party_text: The RPD did not believe that CIC was in possession of the document.
result.why: The court states the RPD did not believe CIC had the document.

result.party_text: Considering the importance of this evidence for the applicant’s narrative, the RPD held that his inability to produce it negatively affected his credibility.
result.why: The court confirms the RPD held the inability to produce the diploma negatively affected credibility.

result.party_text: The RPD did not believe that the applicant’s birth certificate was sufficient to demonstrate his identity.
result.why: The court states the RPD did not believe the birth certificate was sufficient to demonstrate identity.

result.party_text: Despite not being satisfied with his identity demonstration, the RPD continued with its analysis, concluding that even had the applicant sufficiently demonstrated his identity, his refugee claim would still have been denied because it lacked credibility.
result.why: The court confirms the RPD continued analysis despite identity doubts and would have denied claim for lack of credibility.

result.party_text: The RPD drew negative inferences from the fact that the applicant had amended his original Basis of Claim form [BOC] to reflect that his father’s stroke occurred between his two arrests (and not following his second arrest).
result.why: The court states the RPD drew negative inferences from the amendment to the BOC form.

result.party_text: The Board considered this to be a significant event in the applicant’s life, and so he should not have made a chronological error in this respect.
result.why: The court accepts the Board's view that the applicant should not have made a chronological error regarding his father's stroke.

result.party_text: The RPD also drew negative inferences as it seemingly misunderstood the difference between a heart attack and a stroke.
result.why: The court acknowledges the RPD's negative inference due to misunderstanding the difference between a heart attack and a stroke.

result.party_text: The applicant had written in his BOC that his father had suffered a stroke, and had produced a medical report indicating that his father had suffered from facial paralysis in late November 2012, and was advised to seek bed rest for five days.
result.why: The court accepts that the applicant wrote about his father's stroke and produced a medical report indicating facial paralysis and bed rest advice.

result.party_text: Yet the RPD could not accept that a man suffering from a heart condition would be issued such a medical report.
result.why: The court accepts that the RPD did not accept that a man with a heart condition would be issued such a medical report.

result.party_text: The applicant had testified that his father became bedridden, almost paralyzed, and required assistance to complete basic life tasks; yet the medical note does not mention a bedridden person, but rather someone who suffers from facial paralysis and who has to stay in bed for a five-day period.
result.why: The court accepts the RPD's observation about the discrepancy between the applicant's testimony and the medical note regarding bedridden status.

result.party_text: The RPD also did not believe that the applicant had to go to the hospital following the torture he suffered when first detained, as the medical note he produced (and the list of drugs it claims were administered to him) does not corroborate his allegations.
result.why: The court accepts the RPD's disbelief that the applicant had to go to hospital following torture based on the medical note and drugs list.

result.party_text: No explanation was provided as to why these specific drugs would not be administered to a torture victim.
result.why: The court notes no explanation was provided about the drugs not being administered to a torture victim.

result.party_text: Even had the applicant established his identity and been considered credible, he had an internal flight alternative [IFA] in Mumbai, Delhi or Bangalore.
result.why: The court states the applicant had an internal flight alternative in Mumbai, Delhi or Bangalore.

result.party_text: The applicant appealed this decision to the RAD, invoking three main grounds: (1) the RPD erred in analyzing his identity; (2) the RPD did not properly evaluate his credibility; and (3) the RPD erred in its IFA analysis.
result.why: The court acknowledges the applicant appealed on three main grounds as stated.

result.party_text: The applicant's appeal was rejected by a one member panel of the RAD on September 26, 2013.
result.why: The court confirms the applicant's appeal was rejected by a one member panel of the RAD.

result.party_text: The applicant sought to produce his 2002 high school diploma before the RAD as new evidence under subsection 110(4) of the Act.
result.why: The court notes the applicant sought to produce his 2002 high school diploma as new evidence before the RAD.

result.party_text: The applicant submitted a written statement explaining how his documentary evidence met the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act.
result.why: The court states the applicant submitted a written statement explaining how his evidence met subsection 110(4) requirements.

result.party_text: The RAD determined that subsection 110(4) is very similar to paragraph 113(a) of the Act, which deals with admissibility of fresh evidence before a PRRA officer.
result.why: The court confirms the RAD's determination about subsection 110(4) and paragraph 113(a) similarity.

result.party_text: The RAD applied the criteria from Raza v Canada, evaluating credibility, relevance, newness, and materiality of the evidence to decide on admissibility.
result.why: The court confirms the RAD applied Raza criteria to evaluate evidence admissibility.

result.party_text: The applicant argued he only became aware on June 11, 2013 that the diploma had been faxed on February 25, 2013 by CIC to his former lawyer, making it impossible to produce before the RPD.
result.why: The court acknowledges the applicant's claim about awareness timing and impossibility to produce the document before RPD.

result.party_text: The applicant argued he needed the diploma for his appeal to prove the RPD erred in not believing that CIC had seized it.
result.why: The court records the applicant's argument about needing the diploma to prove RPD error.

result.party_text: The applicant argued that failure to produce the diploma negatively affected his overall credibility and it was paramount to have it before the RAD.
result.why: The court notes the applicant's argument about the diploma's importance to his credibility before the RAD.

result.party_text: The RAD concluded that the applicant could have produced the document at the RPD hearing date, so it was not admissible before the RAD.
result.why: The court states the RAD concluded the document could have been produced at the RPD hearing, so inadmissible before RAD.

result.party_text: The RAD presumed the applicant had been made aware of the document’s retrieval from CIC because he had not taken a complaint procedure against his former lawyer for failing to advise him.
result.why: The RAD presumed the applicant was aware of the document's retrieval because he did not complain about his lawyer's failure to advise him.

result.party_text: The RAD dismissed the applicant’s request for a hearing under subsection 110(6) of the Act to reassess credibility in light of the diploma production.
result.why: The RAD dismissed the applicant's request for a hearing under subsection 110(6) to reassess credibility.

result.party_text: Since the document was deemed inadmissible, the RAD found no ground to hold a hearing.
result.why: The RAD found no ground to hold a hearing since the document was deemed inadmissible.

result.party_text: The RAD noted that a Quebec Bar member owes duties of competence, loyalty, integrity, independence, disinterest, diligence, and prudence to a client.
result.why: The RAD noted the duties owed by a Quebec Bar member to a client.

result.party_text: The applicant did not claim his former lawyer acted incompetently nor provide proof of a complaint against her.
result.why: The applicant did not claim incompetence nor provide proof of a complaint against his former lawyer.

result.party_text: The RAD reviewed the three grounds of appeal (identity, credibility, IFA) on the reasonableness standard.
result.why: The RAD reviewed the three grounds of appeal on the reasonableness standard.

result.party_text: The RAD held that the RPD unreasonably concluded the applicant failed to satisfactorily demonstrate his identity.
result.why: The RAD held the RPD unreasonably concluded the applicant failed to demonstrate identity.

result.party_text: The RAD noted its role is not to re-evaluate evidence or do a microscopic analysis but to determine if the outcome was reasonable.
result.why: The RAD noted its role is not to re-evaluate evidence or do microscopic analysis but to determine if the outcome was reasonable.

result.party_text: The RAD agreed the applicant failed to make sufficient efforts to provide identity documents and the RPD was right to draw a negative credibility finding on that.
result.why: The RAD agreed the applicant failed to provide identity documents and the RPD was right to draw a negative credibility finding.

result.party_text: The RAD found it unreasonable that the RPD did not consider the probative value of the school diploma and 1998 report card in assessing identity, though it assessed the documents for other reasons.
result.why: The RAD found it unreasonable that the RPD did not consider the probative value of the school diploma and report card in assessing identity.

result.party_text: The RAD determined the RPD’s overall credibility assessment was reasonable.
result.why: The RAD determined the RPD’s overall credibility assessment was reasonable.

result.party_text: The RAD did not address the RPD’s determination on the applicant’s IFA because the applicant was deemed not credible.
result.why: The RAD did not address the RPD’s determination on the applicant’s IFA because the applicant was deemed not credible.

result.party_text: The RAD owes the RPD deference and should review the RPD decision applying the reasonableness standard.
result.why: The court explicitly disagrees that the RAD owes the RPD deference and should apply the reasonableness standard.

result.party_text: The RAD’s determination of the appropriate analysis for assessing admissibility of new evidence should be reviewed on a reasonableness standard as it involves the tribunal applying its home statute, while errors of law are generally reviewed on a correctness standard.
result.why: The court records the respondent's argument that the RAD's determination should be reviewed on a reasonableness standard as it involves applying its home statute.

result.party_text: The exceptions to the reasonableness standard requiring correctness review apply only to constitutional questions, questions of central importance to the legal system as a whole outside the adjudicator’s expertise, jurisdictional lines between competing tribunals, and true questions of jurisdiction or vires.
result.why: The court accepts the respondent's statement of exceptions to reasonableness review requiring correctness review.

result.party_text: The admissibility of new evidence before the RAD is within the tribunal’s expertise and does not involve a question of central importance to the legal system or special circumstances requiring correctness review.
result.why: The court agrees with the respondent that admissibility of new evidence is within the tribunal's expertise and does not require correctness review.

result.party_text: The RAD failed to admit the 2002 school diploma, which was core to the applicant's story and credibility, gravely prejudicing his claim.
result.why: The court acknowledges the applicant's argument that the RAD failed to admit the diploma, which was core to his story and credibility.

result.party_text: The RAD failed to properly apply the Raza test to the new evidence, which met all its criteria.
result.why: The court notes the applicant's argument that the RAD failed to properly apply the Raza test to the new evidence.

result.party_text: The RAD could not have reasonably expected the applicant to produce the diploma at the RPD hearing.
result.answer_quote: The applicant was required to establish that he could not have reasonably been expected to provide the newly submitted documents at his RPD hearing. The respondent maintains the RAD did not err in finding that he failed to do so.
result.why: The court states the applicant argues the diploma could not reasonably be expected at the RPD hearing, but the respondent contends the applicant failed to establish this.

result.party_text: The diploma was critically probative as it proved the applicant attended school with Bhupinder Singh and was truthful about it.
result.why: The court records the applicant's argument that the diploma was critically probative as it proved attendance with Bhupinder Singh and truthfulness.

result.party_text: The RPD did not believe the applicant's testimony about the diploma being seized by CBSA, but it was true, showing he was not lying.
result.why: The court notes the applicant's argument that the RPD did not believe the testimony about the diploma seizure, which was true and showed honesty.

result.party_text: The RAD blamed the applicant for failure to produce the document despite recognizing it was the lawyer's fault, unfairly prejudicing the applicant who likely did not know about the missing document.
result.why: The court records the applicant's argument that the RAD blamed him despite recognizing the lawyer's fault, unfairly prejudicing him.

result.party_text: The RAD used the proper test by interpreting subsection 110(4) in light of paragraph 113(a), and the Raza factors apply.
result.why: The court states the respondent's argument that the RAD used the proper test and that Raza factors apply.

result.party_text: The applicant was required to establish he could not reasonably have been expected to provide the new documents at the RPD hearing, which he failed to do.
result.why: The court states the respondent's position that the applicant failed to establish the required expectation regarding new documents.

result.party_text: A restrictive interpretation of subsection 110(4) would limit a claimant's ability to obtain a full fact-based appeal as intended by the former Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
result.answer_quote: The vast majority of claimants who are coming from countries that do normally produce refugees would for the first time, if rejected at the refugee protection division, have access to a full fact-based appeal at the refugee appeal division of the IRB. [Emphasis added.]
result.why: The court agrees that a restrictive interpretation would limit a claimant's ability to obtain a full fact-based appeal as intended.

result.party_text: Evidence at stake is often essential to prove the factual basis of errors alleged by the claimant against the RPD.
result.why: The court accepts that evidence is often essential to prove factual errors alleged by the claimant.

result.party_text: Given the strict timelines for submitting evidence before the RPD, the RAD should have leeway to allow claimants to respond to evidentiary deficiencies raised by the RPD.
result.why: The court accepts that the RAD should have leeway to allow claimants to respond to evidentiary deficiencies due to strict timelines.

result.party_text: The four implied questions from paragraph 113(a) of the Act (credibility, relevance, newness, materiality) are specific to PRRA applications and should not be transferred to appeals before the RAD.
result.why: The court accepts that the four implied questions are specific to PRRA applications and should not be transferred to RAD appeals.

result.party_text: The evidence at issue was material to demonstrate errors in two key credibility findings by the RPD regarding the confiscation of a diploma and the applicant's school attendance with Bhupinder Singh.
result.why: The court accepts that the evidence was material to demonstrate errors in key credibility findings by the RPD.

result.party_text: The RAD recognized that the failure to produce the document was the fault of the lawyer who failed to forward it after receiving it from CBSA.
result.why: The court accepts that the RAD recognized the failure to produce the document was the lawyer's fault.

result.party_text: The respondent proposed a question of general importance for certification, with the consent of the applicant, regarding whether the RAD owes deference to RPD findings of fact and mixed fact and law under the RAD's statutory framework.
result.answer_quote: As indicated above, I am of the view that said question is not determinative of the present case and that it would not be determinative of an appeal. However, I view the following questions as being of general importance and determinative in the case at bar: • What standard of review should be applied by this Court when reviewing the Refugee Appeal Division’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27? • In considering the role of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment officer and that of the Refugee Appeal Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board, sitting in appeal of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division, does the test set out in Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 for the interpretation of paragraph 113(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 apply to its subsection 110(4)?
result.why: The court finds the proposed question not determinative and instead certifies different questions of general importance.
